questions.q: What does the offline store hold that the online store does not?
options: The full historical record of feature values across time, not just the latest value
A password vault for the model registry
The model's trained weights
A list of all entity IDs ever seen, with no feature values
questions.explain: The offline store keeps every historical value for every entity over time, which is what training needs; the online store keeps only the current value per entity.

questions.q: Why are online stores almost always backed by Redis, DynamoDB, or similar key-value systems rather than a data warehouse?
options: Data warehouses cannot store numeric data
Online lookups need single-digit millisecond latency for one entity at a time, which is exactly what key-value stores are optimized for
Key-value stores are always cheaper regardless of workload
Data warehouses are only used for offline storage by law
questions.explain: The online store's access pattern — one fast lookup by entity key, no history — matches what key-value stores are built for; warehouses are optimized for large historical scans instead.

questions.q: In Feast's feature_store.yaml, what do the `offline_store` and `online_store` sections represent?
options: Two completely separate feature definitions that must be kept in sync manually
Configuration for where each store's data lives — the same FeatureView works against either without being rewritten
A list of model hyperparameters
User authentication credentials for the Feast UI
questions.explain: The YAML file configures storage backends, not feature logic. The same FeatureView definition from Lesson 5 works unchanged whichever offline or online store is configured.

questions.q: What does Feast's `feast materialize-incremental` command do?
options: Deletes all historical data from the offline store
Copies feature values that changed since the last run from the offline store into the online store
Trains a new model from scratch
Switches the online store from Redis to DynamoDB automatically
questions.explain: Materialization is the bridge from offline to online: materialize-incremental copies only what's changed since the last run, keeping the online store fresh without recomputing everything.

questions.q: If a feature needs to reflect an event that happened only a few seconds ago, why might scheduled materialization not be sufficient?
options: Scheduled materialization runs on an interval (minutes to hours), which is too slow for sub-second freshness — a streaming path is needed instead
Materialization is always instantaneous regardless of schedule
Feast does not support any form of materialization
Online stores cannot be updated outside of training time
questions.explain: Scheduled materialization has a freshness lag tied to its run interval. When near-real-time freshness is required, teams add a streaming path that writes directly into the online store, bypassing the batch schedule.
